title: SYSK Selects: How the Placebo Effect Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on the placebo effect. Josh introduces it as a favorite. The hosts cover the etymology of "placebo" (from hired mourners, then "I shall please"), early history (Thomas Jefferson's "pious fraud," 1811 Quincy definition, John Haygarth, Henry Beecher's WWII saline-for-morphine observation and the double-blind study), definitions of placebo and placebo effect, expectancy and classical conditioning explanations, brain imaging and endorphin/dopamine research, the nocebo effect, Ted Kaptchuk's ritual-based research, doctors prescribing placebos and AMA guidance, skeptical criticisms, Obaplac children's placebo, and listener mail thanking staff and a listener from Perth.

segments.title: Selects intro and placebo word origin
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as his Selects pick. The hosts discuss the origin of the word placebo, from hired mourners at funerals and the Latin 'I shall please.'

segments.title: Ted Kaptchuk and double-blind history
segments.summary: The hosts describe Ted Kaptchuk's path from acupuncturist to Harvard placebo researcher and his 2001 New England Journal of Medicine criticism over control groups. They then cover Henry Beecher's WWII saline observation and the rise of double-blind placebo trials.

segments.title: Early placebo history
segments.summary: The hosts cover early references to placebos, including an 1811 Quincy definition, Thomas Jefferson's 1807 'pious fraud' note on bread pills, John Haygarth's early studies, and 1930s and 1940s research.

segments.title: Defining placebo effect and psychological explanations
segments.summary: The hosts define the placebo and placebo effect, note that pills, injections, fake surgery and inert treatments can work, and describe the early view that placebo effects were purely psychological. They discuss subject expectancy and observer expectancy effects and classical conditioning.

segments.title: Physiological evidence: brain imaging, endorphins and dopamine
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2002 UCLA study of antidepressant trials with EEG brain monitoring, a 1970s dental study showing endorphin blocking reduces placebo response, a 2004 University of Michigan endorphin study, and research linking placebo response to dopamine and genetics.

segments.title: Nocebo effect
segments.summary: The hosts explain the nocebo effect, where people on inert pills experience side effects, and give an example of chemotherapy patients feeling nauseated in a room with a familiar color.

segments.title: Ritual, expectation and Kaptchuk's research
segments.summary: The hosts describe Kaptchuk's view that placebo response relies on ritual, including bedside manner, perceived cost and perceived effectiveness of a pill, and his 'schmaltzy' care study. They also discuss how telling patients about a drug affects its efficacy.

segments.title: Hypochondria anecdote and Obaplac
segments.summary: Chuck shares a story about an emergency room visit where a nurse called him a hypochondriac. The hosts then discuss Obaplac, a children's placebo marketed in 2008, and childhood memories of orange children's aspirin.

segments.title: Criticisms, doctors prescribing placebos and AMA guidance
segments.summary: The hosts cover skeptical criticisms, including hypochondria, natural recovery and the need for no-treatment groups. They discuss surveys showing doctors prescribe placebos, the 2006 AMA guideline that patients must be informed and agree, and ethical concerns about deception.

segments.title: Listener mail: staff shout-outs and Alex from Perth
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank staff including Rebecca, Sherry and Joe. They read listener mail from Alex in Perth, Western Australia, who says the show helped him through job searching and mining downturn.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact details and sign off.
